title: ReFactX: Scalable Reasoning with Reliable Facts via Constrained Generation
sections: Problem

LLMs hallucinate and lack knowledge outside their training data. Retrieval-augmented generation and tool use help but depend on retrievers, entity linkers or extra services, which add pipeline complexity and propagate errors.
Method

ReFactX indexes knowledge-graph facts in a prefix tree and uses constrained decoding: when the model emits a Fact command, decoding is restricted to token sequences that complete an existing fact; otherwise generation is unconstrained. Wikidata truthy triples are verbalised and tokenised; the index holds more than 800 million facts stored in PostgreSQL (about 95 GB). Prompting is two-shot in-context learning with beam search over 3 beams. The models are not fine-tuned to use the tool.
Datasets
Mintaka, a 200-question development sample of 2WikiMultiHopQA, a 200-question sample of WebQSP, and a proprietary financial Bank dataset of 278 questions over about 10K triples.
Results

Evaluated with exact match and LLM-as-a-judge (Table 2). On 2WikiMultiHopQA, Qwen2.5-72B with ReFactX reaches precision 96.4 and accuracy 92.5 versus 45.0 accuracy for the LLM alone; Llama-3.3-70B reaches 81.0 versus 56.5. On Mintaka, ReFactX accuracy is lower than the LLM alone (Llama 56.0 versus 82.0). On WebQSP, Qwen2.5-72B scores 65.5 versus 73.0 for the LLM alone. On the Bank dataset the best precision is 51.3 (Phi-4) and accuracy reaches 42.8. Constrained generation adds about 1.3 percent time overhead: 303.89 s versus 300.14 s for 4,000 tokens (Figure 6).
Limitations

Weak on count and superlative questions: Bank count questions score under 10 percent and Mintaka superlatives 14.3 percent (Llama). Facts must be generated left to right starting from known information, ordinal multi-hop questions are hard, and cross-paper comparisons in Table 3 use different samples and metrics.

title: Aligning Knowledge Graphs and Language Models for Factual Accuracy
sections: Problem

LLMs give wrong or stale answers to entity-centric factual questions. Fine-tuning on knowledge-graph text or retrieval augmentation loses relational structure or confuses entities with similar names; a motivating example is ownership chains between companies.
Method

ALIGNed-LLM injects knowledge-graph structure into a language model. Entity embeddings from a frozen pre-trained TransE model pass through a trainable projection layer (identity, linear, or MLP with GELU) and are concatenated with the token embeddings of the query. Training has two stages: first only the projection layer is trained, then the model is fine-tuned end to end with LoRA. Baselines are the same LLMs fine-tuned on textual question-answer pairs from the graph.
Datasets
Wikidata questions derived from Wikidata5M, Mintaka, YAGO3-10, and a proprietary Company Ownership (CO) dataset from a European central bank with about 29k entities and 100k triples.
Results

Exact match for Mistral-7B on Wikidata rises from 0.221 to 0.605. TinyLlama-1.1B improves by 11.3 points on Wikidata and 13.5 points exact match on CO, while Vicuna-13B on Wikidata improves by only 0.7. Gains on Mintaka are smaller (about 1.3 to 5.6). Paired t-tests find 22 of 24 comparisons significant. On CO a linear projection beats a more complex projection by about 5.3 exact-match points, which the authors relate to the sparsity of that graph; 1024-dimensional embeddings give slightly higher scores.
Limitations
Gains are uneven across models and datasets, the best projection depends on graph topology, queries are assumed to centre on one reference entity, and the CO dataset is not public.

title: SMART: Relation-Aware Learning of Geometric Representations for Knowledge Graphs
sections: Problem

Most knowledge graph embedding models apply one elementary geometric transformation, or one fixed combination, to every relation, which cannot capture the mix of relational patterns (symmetry, non-commutativity, hierarchy) in real graphs such as company-ownership networks.
Method

SMART combines four elementary geometric transformations: translation, rotation, reflection and scaling. It learns relation-specific attention weights over them in three phases: training with equal weights, adaptive learning of the weights, and freezing in which only the top transformation per relation is kept. Variant SMART assigns each relation its top transformation; SMART_m uses majority voting across relations.
Datasets
WN18RR, FB15k-237, YouTube and a private company ownership knowledge graph (COKG).
Results

MRR (x1000) at dimension 32: on WN18RR SMART scores 449 plus or minus 2 and SMART_m 438, while the best baseline scores 463. On FB15k-237 SMART scores 274 and SMART_m 298 against 313 for MuRE. On YouTube (dimension 300) SMART scores 294 against 320 for ComplEx. On COKG (dimension 100) SMART scores 550 against 489 for RotatE. A phase ablation on WN18RR shows MRR rising from 397 (training only) to 446 (adaptive) to 449 (full), but freezing hurts on FB15k-237.
Limitations

Composite-transformation baselines beat SMART on several WN18RR and FB15k-237 metrics, translation receives almost no weight on WN18RR and COKG, the fixed transformation ordering biases results, and high-dimensional hyperparameter search is expensive.

title: Loss-Aware Pattern Inference: A Correction on the Wrongly Claimed Limitations of Embedding Models
sections: Problem

Several papers claim that TransE and its successors (TransH, TransR, STransE, FTransE) cannot encode certain relation patterns, for example that TransE cannot encode symmetric or reflexive relations, a claim also made in the RotatE paper. This paper argues those proofs are unsound.
Argument

The earlier proofs assume that h + r equals t exactly, a zero residual. The losses actually used for training, such as the margin ranking loss and the RotatE loss, only bound the score of positive triples from above and never enforce exact equality. The authors define four conditions, from a strict zero residual to triple-specific margins, and prove that under the looser conditions TransE can encode symmetric and reflexive patterns when the margin is chosen appropriately (for symmetry the upper bound gamma1 must exceed the norm of r). The limitations therefore depend on the loss function, not only on the scoring function.
Experiments

TransE in real and complex space was trained with several margin-based losses and the RotatE loss using PyTorch, Adagrad and adversarial negative sampling, on FB15k-237 and WN18RR with embedding dimension 300, evaluated with filtered MR, MRR and Hits@10. Histograms of residual norms check the conditions empirically.
Results

On FB15k-237, TransE with gamma1 = 0 reaches MRR 27.4 and Hits@10 45.7; with loss 4 it reaches MRR 32.3 and Hits@10 52.1; complex TransE with loss 4 reaches MRR 32.8; RotatE with loss 4 reaches MRR 33.0. On WN18RR, TransE with gamma1 = 0 reaches MRR 19.3; with loss 4 MRR 23.5; complex TransE with loss 4 MRR 44.3; RotatE with loss 4 MRR 47.8 and Hits@10 56.9.

title: RotatE: Knowledge Graph Embedding by Relational Rotation in Complex Space
sections: Method

RotatE embeds entities and relations in complex vector space and models each relation as an element-wise rotation from the head to the tail entity, with relation moduli constrained to 1, inspired by Euler's identity. It introduces self-adversarial negative sampling, which samples negatives according to the current model instead of training a separate generator as in GAN-based approaches.
Relation patterns

The paper argues that RotatE can model and infer symmetry and antisymmetry, inversion and composition. In its comparison table TransE models antisymmetry, inversion and composition but not symmetry; DistMult models only symmetry; ComplEx models symmetry, antisymmetry and inversion but not composition. RotatE is presented as the only model covering all of these patterns.
Experiments
Link prediction on FB15k, WN18, FB15k-237 and WN18RR, and the Countries benchmark for composition. The paper reports that RotatE outperforms prior state-of-the-art models on these benchmarks.

title: Convolutional 2D Knowledge Graph Embeddings
sections: Method

ConvE reshapes subject and relation embeddings into 2D grids, applies 2D convolution with 3x3 filters, projects to the embedding dimension and scores all candidate objects with an inner product (1-N scoring), which speeds up evaluation roughly 300 times. ConvE at 1.89M parameters reaches MRR 0.32 on FB15k-237 while DistMult with the same parameter count reaches 0.23.
Test set leakage

WN18 and FB15k contain test triples that can be recovered by inverting training triples: if (cat, hypernym, feline) is in training, the test triple (feline, hyponym, cat) is trivial. The authors build a simple rule-based inverse model that detects inverse relation pairs from training co-occurrence and predicts test triples from their inverses; this model reaches state-of-the-art results on WN18 and FB15k, showing that these benchmarks mostly measure inverse-relation lookup.
WN18RR

The authors release WN18RR, a version of WN18 with inverse relations removed so that it cannot be solved by such a rule. It has 93,003 triples, 40,943 entities and 11 relations. They recommend FB15k-237, WN18RR and YAGO3-10 instead of FB15k and WN18.

title: A Re-evaluation of Knowledge Graph Completion Methods
sections: Problem

Several neural knowledge graph completion models report large gains that do not hold across datasets. The cause is the evaluation protocol: many candidate triples receive exactly the same score as the correct triple, and how ties are broken changes the reported rank. In ConvKB and CapsE, ReLU layers zero out most neurons so different triples collapse to the same score; in one FB15k-237 example 8,520 of 14,541 negatives tied with the correct triple.
Protocols

TOP places the correct triple first among ties, which rewards constant-score models; BOTTOM places it last, which is overly harsh; RANDOM places it at a random position among ties and is the recommended protocol.
Results

MRR on FB15k-237, originally reported versus RANDOM protocol: ConvE 0.325 versus 0.324; RotatE 0.338 versus 0.336; TuckER 0.358 versus 0.353; ConvKB 0.396 versus 0.243; CapsE 0.523 versus 0.150; KBAT 0.518 versus 0.157 (KBAT also had a test-leakage bug that was fixed). Under TOP, ConvKB reaches 0.407 and CapsE 0.511; under BOTTOM they fall to 0.130 and 0.134.
Recommendations
Use the RANDOM tie-breaking protocol, report how many negatives tie with the correct triple, check implementations for data leakage, and report mean and standard deviation over multiple seeds.

title: The ARC of Progress towards AGI: A Living Survey of Abstraction and Reasoning
sections: Scope

A living survey of 82 approaches across three versions of the ARC-AGI benchmark and the ARC Prize 2024 and 2025 competitions, covering program synthesis, neuro-symbolic and neural methods. The first release covers the field as of February 2026.
Findings

Every paradigm scores roughly 2 to 3 times lower on ARC-AGI-2 than on ARC-AGI-1, pointing to limits in compositional generalisation. Top systems score 93.0 percent on ARC-AGI-1, 68.8 percent on ARC-AGI-2 and 13 percent on ARC-AGI-3, while humans remain near perfect on all versions. Cost per task fell about 390 times in one year, though much of this reflects reduced test-time parallelism. Small resource-constrained entries sometimes compete with very large models. Test-time adaptation and refinement loops appear key; compositional reasoning and interactive learning remain unsolved.

title: Are Researchers Being Replaced by Artificial Intelligence?
sections: Argument

A perspective essay arguing that replacement of researchers is already under way, not as disappearance but as a shift from researcher-as-creator to researcher-as-curator, where humans keep responsibility while losing intellectual ownership. It surveys AI research tools across the scientific lifecycle and examines ethical, legal, skilling, validation and technical risks.
Evidence

The evidence is drawn from literature, news, policies and informal sources rather than a systematic study. Figures cited include a 2023 Nature survey of 1,600 researchers, an analysis suggesting that 21 percent of ICLR reviews may be AI-generated, hundreds of hallucinated references in more than 50 accepted NeurIPS 2025 papers, and 33,540 active ICML 2026 abstracts. The authors frame risks at their upper bound.
Conclusion
Researchers must retain judgement, accountability and understanding; without governance, skills and validation capacity, science risks knowing that methods work without knowing how.

title: SCI-IDEA: Context-Aware Scientific Ideation Using Token and Sentence Embeddings
sections: Method

SCI-IDEA retrieves a researcher's papers and related work, extracts facets (purpose, mechanism, evaluation, future work), identifies research gaps and generates ideas with zero-shot, chain-of-thought and few-shot prompts. Novelty is one minus the maximum cosine similarity to other ideas; surprise is the negative log-likelihood under a pretrained model. Ideas above both thresholds are flagged as Aha moments and refined with human feedback.
Data and evaluation

100 researcher profiles from top computer-science venues with publications from CORE, arXiv and Semantic Scholar. Ideas are scored 1 to 10 for novelty, excitement, feasibility and effectiveness by LLM judges and by PhD-level human reviewers.
Results

Without embeddings GPT-4o zero-shot reaches an average LLM-judged score of 6.88; with token embeddings DeepSeek-32B 2-shot reaches 6.89; with sentence embeddings GPT-4o 5-shot and DeepSeek-70B 5-shot both reach 6.87. Human scores are much lower and more variable: GPT-4o 2-shot receives 4.25 from humans versus 6.84 from the LLM judge, and DeepSeek-70B 5-shot receives 1 from humans on all dimensions.
Limitations
Quality depends on the input papers, evaluation is limited to computer science with a small human panel, iterative refinement is costly, and LLM judges overestimate quality.
